slides.say: m and n are positive integers, and m plus n is odd. Which of the following is true about the expression m to the power of n, plus n to the power of m, plus nine, plus four n?

So m plus n is odd. One of m and n must be even and the other odd, because two evens or two odds add up to an even number. We need to know whether the whole expression is even or odd. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, checking the numbers before raising them to powers, and then plugging in the two possible cases.

[short pause] Let's start with the powers. m and n are positive integers, so the powers are positive whole numbers. Raising a number to one of these powers keeps it even or odd. So, just to check even and odd, replace m to the power of n with m, and n to the power of m with n. We now check m plus n, plus nine, plus four n. This simpler expression has the same even-or-odd result as the original one.

m plus n is odd, from the given. Nine is odd too. Four n is even because four times any integer is even. The two odd parts add up to an even number. Adding the even part keeps the answer even. So the original expression is always even, and choice number one is our answer.
at: choice number one is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's try plugging in. Start with m is one and n is two. Their sum is odd, so they fit. One squared is one, two to the power of one is two, and four n is eight. One plus two plus nine plus eight is twenty, which is even. Check the choices now. Choice number two says the result is odd when m is odd and n is even. Our example fits that case and gives an even result, so choice number two is out. Choice number four says always odd, so it is out too.
at: m is one and n is two

slides.say: Choices one and three remain. Choice number three talks about the other case, m even and n odd, so choose m is two and n is one. Two to the power of one is two, one squared is one, and four n is four. Two plus one plus nine plus four is sixteen, which is even, not odd. So choice number three is out. Only choice number one remains, always even. We can stop. Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: m is two and n is one
